reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A fibro-inflammatory process in the retroperitoneum that encases the aorta, iliac vessels, and ureters, most often around the infrarenal aorta
Presents insidiously with poorly localised back, flank, or abdominal pain, constitutional symptoms, and raised inflammatory markers
Ureteric entrapment causes obstructive uropathy and may present with renal impairment or anuria
A substantial proportion falls within the spectrum of IgG4-related disease, so serum IgG4 and histology for IgG4-positive plasma cells are informative
Secondary causes include malignancy, certain drugs, radiotherapy, infection, and prior surgery, which must be excluded before labelling it idiopathic
Cross-sectional imaging shows a periaortic soft-tissue rind that characteristically does not displace the aorta anteriorly, unlike lymphoma
First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids, often with a steroid-sparing agent, alongside relief of ureteric obstruction
reference.pathophysiology: Retroperitoneal fibrosis is characterised by a chronic inflammatory and fibrotic plaque in the retroperitoneum, frequently centred on the abdominal aorta (chronic periaortitis). Many idiopathic cases represent a manifestation of IgG4-related disease, with an immune-mediated infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils driving progressive collagen deposition. An exaggerated inflammatory response to atherosclerotic aortic antigens has also been proposed. The expanding fibrous tissue encases and constricts adjacent structures, most importantly the ureters, producing obstructive uropathy and hydronephrosis.
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis to characterise the periaortic mass and detect ureteric involvement and hydronephrosis
Renal function tests and imaging to assess obstructive uropathy
Serum IgG4 and total immunoglobulins to assess for IgG4-related disease
Image-guided biopsy in atypical cases to exclude malignancy and confirm IgG4-rich fibrosis
PET imaging to assess disease activity and exclude a malignant or infective cause
redFlags: Acute kidney injury or anuria from bilateral ureteric obstruction
Features suggesting underlying malignancy such as marked weight loss or atypical imaging
Anterior displacement of the aorta on imaging raising concern for lymphoma
Vascular compromise from encasement of major arteries or veins
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic and IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis generally responds well to corticosteroids with regression of the mass and relief of obstruction, though relapse is common and long-term monitoring of renal function is needed; malignancy-associated disease carries the prognosis of the underlying tumour.
pitfalls: Labelling the disease idiopathic without excluding malignancy, drugs, and infection
Missing silent bilateral ureteric obstruction and progressive renal failure
Overlooking a diagnosis of IgG4-related disease and its multi-organ implications
Assuming a periaortic mass is inflammatory when imaging features suggest lymphoma
Relieving obstruction without treating the underlying inflammatory process
management: Induce remission with corticosteroids, the mainstay for idiopathic and IgG4-related disease, achieving regression of the periaortic mass
Add steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as methotrexate, mycophenolate, azathioprine or tamoxifen, or rituximab, for relapsing or refractory disease
Relieve ureteric obstruction promptly with ureteric stenting or percutaneous nephrostomy to protect renal function
Exclude and treat secondary causes including malignancy, drugs, radiotherapy and infection before labelling the disease idiopathic
Consider ureterolysis or surgical release for entrapped ureters that do not respond to medical therapy
Monitor renal function, inflammatory markers and serial imaging for relapse during and after treatment
Coordinate care between rheumatology, nephrology and urology for combined medical and interventional management
